My ranking:

Name	Impression

For a Leftium/... repo, I'd probably use:

Leftium/pages-kit

with README title:

GitHub Pages Deployment Kit

One documented, versioned way to deploy my projects to GitHub Pages.

I would structure it like this
pages-kit/
├── README.md
├── CHANGELOG.md
├── pages.yml
├── consumers.yml
├── docs/
│   ├── anatomy.md
│   ├── setup.md
│   └── migrations/
│       ├── v1-to-v2.md
│       └── v2-to-v3.md
└── scripts/
    └── check-consumers.ts

pages.yml is the canonical template.

consumers.yml records deployments:

YAML
projects:
  ph:
    repo: Leftium/ph
    version: v2
    workflow: .github/workflows/pages.yml

  weather-sense:
    repo: Leftium/weather-sense
    version: v3
    workflow: .github/workflows/pages.yml

  hn:
    repo: Leftium/hn
    version: v3
    workflow: .github/workflows/pages.yml

I'd use the word consumer rather than projects.yml because it makes the relationship clear to both humans and agents: these repos consume this template.

And put something machine-readable directly in every copied workflow:

YAML
# pages-kit: Leftium/pages-kit@v3
# docs: https://github.com/Leftium/pages-kit

That gives an agent a very easy invariant:

Never modify this workflow without checking the referenced pages-kit version first.

It also lets check-consumers.ts query every listed repository and compare the declared version/hash with the registry.

But I would seriously consider not copying most of pages.yml

The cleaner version of this project is probably a versioned reusable workflow.

A consuming repo could contain something conceptually like:

YAML
name: Deploy Pages

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

jobs:
  deploy:
    uses: Leftium/pages-kit/.github/workflows/pages.yml@v3
    with:
      build-command: pnpm build
      output-directory: build

GitHub allows reusable workflows to be referenced by branch, tag, or SHA; a SHA gives strongest immutability, while something like @v3 gives you convenient major-version updates. 
GitHub Docs
 An actions/checkout inside the reusable workflow checks out the calling project, not pages-kit, which is exactly what you'd want here. 
GitHub Docs

Then you don't actually have to manually maintain:

project A → v3
project B → v2

because it is encoded directly in every consumer:

YAML
uses: Leftium/pages-kit/.github/workflows/pages.yml@v3

Your consumers.yml can become a registry/audit file, rather than the source of truth.

That architecture feels particularly well suited to what you're building:

Leftium/pages-kit
                 │
        ┌────────┴────────┐
        │ reusable Pages  │
        │ workflow @ v3   │
        └────────┬────────┘
                 │
       ┌─────────┼─────────┐
       ↓         ↓         ↓
      ph       hn      weather-sense
     @v3      @v2          @v3

GitHub also exposes reused workflows as dependencies in its dependency graph, so you're working with GitHub's reuse model instead of inventing an entirely parallel mechanism. 
GitHub Docs

What the README should contain

For your human + agent goal, I wouldn't make the README merely a setup tutorial. I'd make it the specification for how Pages deployment works across your projects:

Purpose / golden path — "Use this workflow unless a project has an explicit reason not to."

Install — exact file/caller to add and GitHub Pages settings to select.

Anatomy of pages.yml — explain on, permissions, concurrency, build, artifact upload, environment, and deploy.

Why each weird bit exists — especially pages: write, id-token: write, github-pages, needs, and cancel-in-progress.

Versions — what v1, v2, v3 mean.

Consumers — current version used by each project.

Updating a consumer — check changelog → apply migration → test Actions → update registry.

Agent instructions — invariants and what an agent may/may not customize.

Troubleshooting — artifact path, base path, CNAME/custom domains, Pages source setting.

Upstream references — GitHub's starter workflow and documentation.

GitHub's own current example is particularly useful for the "what every part does" section because it explicitly explains that on controls triggering, permissions permits publication, environment connects the deployment to Pages and its URL, and the steps check out/configure/upload/deploy. 
GitHub Docs

So my preferred combination would be:

repo: pages-kit
canonical workflow: .github/workflows/pages.yml
consumer registry: consumers.yml
versioning: Git tags such as v1, v2, v3
consumer declaration: uses: Leftium/pages-kit/.github/workflows/pages.yml@v3
README: both tutorial and specification
CHANGELOG/migrations: tells agents precisely how to update old consumers

That gives you something closer to a tiny internal deployment platform than a pile of copied YAML, while still being simple enough to understand completely.

The important new decisions are:

logo is an early post-v0 add-on.

A logo can be a preset, because you have a reusable default logo.

I’d add/replace these sections:

Edit
Logo-related specification updates
Core concept: project-specific source configuration

Some add-ons may consume project-specific source configuration in addition to presets and overrides.

This is distinct from a preset:

preset
  reusable configuration

project source
  project-specific declarative input

override
  final local delta

Example:

logo preset:
  core/logo/leftium-default.json

project source:
  .leftium/logo.json

A project source MAY completely supersede a reusable preset when that better matches the underlying domain.

Native-format presets

Logo presets SHOULD use the native leftium-logo JSON format.

Example:

logo/
├── leftium-default.json
├── rocket.json
└── ...

The JSON describes visual rendering only.

It SHOULD NOT contain unrelated packaging metadata merely to make the format more convenient for leftium.

Post-v0 candidate: logo

Purpose:

Generate and install project logo, favicon, and related branding assets using leftium-logo.

Examples:

le add logo
le add logo --preset leftium-default
le add logo --preset rocket
le add logo --config ./logo.json
Default behavior

Bare:

le add logo

SHOULD use the user's configured default logo preset when available.

For the default Leftium configuration this may resolve to:

logo:leftium-default

This supports using a temporary/default favicon before a project receives custom branding.

Logo presets

A logo preset is a reusable visual configuration.

Example:

core/logo/leftium-default.json

A preset contains the same visual JSON understood by leftium-logo.

Presets may come from:

the core mine

user scope

project scope

configured mines

Example:

le add logo --preset alice/default
Project-specific logo

Once a project has a custom logo, its canonical visual configuration SHOULD be stored as:

.leftium/logo.json

This file contains the native leftium-logo visual configuration.

Example resolution:

default/user logo preset
        ↓
project .leftium/logo.json, if present
        ↓
CLI input/override

A project-specific logo.json SHOULD normally supersede the reusable visual preset rather than requiring the preset and project config to be merged.

Visual config versus packaging metadata

The leftium-logo JSON format represents visual rendering configuration.

Examples include:

icon
colors
background
corner shape/radius
icon size
offset
rotation
favicon-specific rendering

Information used only for packaging or download naming is NOT part of the visual configuration.

For example, a generated Logo Kit may use an app/name value to:

name a ZIP/download

provide convenience metadata in generated files

That does not make the name part of the logo's visual identity.

leftium SHOULD NOT require adding an application/download name to logo.json.

If packaging metadata later becomes necessary, it SHOULD remain a separate input or wrapper around the visual config.

Conceptually:

LogoConfig
  visual recipe

LogoKitOptions
  optional packaging/output metadata

le logo add-on
  installation behavior

Do not introduce LogoKitOptions until an actual use case requires it.

Generation architecture

Preferred long-term architecture:

logo.leftium.com
      │
      │ edits/exports
      ▼
   LogoConfig
      │
      ├──────────────┐
      ▼              ▼
web generator     leftium
                     │
                     ▼
             shared logo renderer
                     │
                     ▼
              generated assets

The website and leftium SHOULD ideally use the same underlying renderer/generation implementation.

Preferred implementation order:

reusable leftium-logo library API, if practical;

local leftium-logo CLI;

remote web service only if necessary.

leftium SHOULD NOT depend on the hosted website when deterministic local generation is practical.

Generated assets

Generated files are installation/build outputs, not the canonical source configuration.

A typical generated Logo Kit may include:

favicon.ico
icon.svg
apple-touch-icon.png
icon-192.png
icon-512.png
logo.png
logo.webp
logo.svg
manifest.webmanifest
head/favicon markup

The exact output set is controlled by leftium-logo and may evolve.

leftium SHOULD install the appropriate generated assets into the detected project's static/public asset location.

Examples:

SvelteKit → static/
Vite      → public/

Other project types MAY require different mappings.

Generated assets MAY be committed to source control.

The normal default SHOULD favor committed generated assets so deployment does not require the logo generator.

Framework integration

le add logo MAY:

detect the project's static/public directory;

generate logo/favicon assets;

install those assets;

update favicon/head references where appropriate;

update or create manifest icon references where appropriate;

preserve unrelated existing manifest/head configuration;

avoid duplicate references;

regenerate idempotently.

Framework integration SHOULD remain separate from logo rendering.

Importing visual configuration

The add-on SHOULD eventually support importing an existing config:

le add logo --config ./logo.json

This may:

validate the config;

copy/store it as:

.leftium/logo.json

generate assets;

install/integrate those assets.

Direct JSON/stdin/share-URL import MAY be supported later.

Update behavior

Because the project logo is declarative, rerunning:

le add logo

SHOULD be idempotent and SHOULD reconcile generated assets with the current visual config.

Future:

le update logo

MAY explicitly regenerate/reconcile logo outputs.

Updated implementation priorities
v0
license
gitattributes
pages
Early post-v0
logo
robots
prettier
knip

logo is a particularly useful early add-on because it proves a capability not covered by v0:

reusable preset
        or
project-specific declarative source
        ↓
external/shared generator
        ↓
generated asset bundle
        ↓
framework-aware installation
Design rule: distinguish source from generated output

When an add-on involves generation:

Store the smallest declarative source needed to reproduce the result.

Do not treat generated output as the canonical preset or configuration when reproducible source exists.

For logo:

canonical:
  leftium-logo JSON

generated:
  PNG / SVG / ICO / WebP / manifest / markup
Design rule: do not expand schemas for installer convenience

leftium SHOULD adapt to an upstream domain model rather than adding unrelated fields to that model solely for installer convenience.

For example:

Do not add an application/download name to the visual logo JSON unless that value becomes semantically part of logo generation itself.

Packaging or installation metadata can remain separate.

One other small conceptual improvement came out of this: preset / project source / override is a useful three-way distinction. gitattributes mostly needs presets + overrides; logo naturally needs presets + project-specific source; other future add-ons may use different combinations. That keeps us from stretching “preset” to mean every possible input.

I think we have enough to save the full spec now. I would not keep expanding the design before implementation.

There are only a handful of things I’d explicitly settle or mark as provisional so an agent doesn’t interpret silence as a decision.

Canonical naming / repo identity. I’d lock this in:

npm package:   leftium
primary CLI:   leftium
short alias:   le
GitHub repo:   Leftium/le
config dir:    .leftium/
extension repo: mine

That gives us stable terminology throughout the spec.

Default preset semantics. We should state that bare le add <addon> may choose an add-on’s configured/default preset:

Bash
le add license
# => default license preset, if configured; otherwise prompt

le add gitattributes
# => default gitattributes preset(s), probably "leftium"

le add logo
# => default logo preset, probably "leftium-default"

And the default itself can come from scope:

built-in → user → project → CLI

So other people aren't forced into your preferences just because the software is called Leftium; they can change their user-level defaults once.

Clarify the three configuration concepts. I think this is important enough to put near the beginning:

preset
  reusable configuration

project source
  project-specific declarative source material

override
  final delta on generated/applied configuration

Examples make it clear:

gitattributes:
  presets + overrides

logo:
  preset OR .leftium/logo.json project source

pages:
  mostly detected/project configuration

Not every add-on has to support all three.

Define what add means when something already exists. I’d explicitly say:

add means “ensure this capability is configured,” not necessarily “create something that does not exist.”

Therefore:

Bash
le add gitattributes

may:

missing       → install
current       → no-op
partial       → complete
customized    → merge/preserve
conflicting   → ask/fail safely

This is important because it makes add naturally idempotent and prevents us from later needing an awkward install vs configure distinction.

Preserve provenance rather than generated-file ownership. Especially with mines/scopes/presets, we should state a principle:

le should be able to explain where effective configuration came from, even when it does not own the whole target file.

Eventually:

Bash
le why gitattributes

might show:

addon:      gitattributes
presets:
  nodiff    user scope
  eol       core mine
override:   .leftium/gitattributes.override

We don't need to implement this in v0, but designing add-ons so provenance isn't destroyed will help later.

Explicitly mark these as unresolved implementation details. I would not decide them before coding:

exact .leftium subdirectory/file naming conventions

exact mine qualification syntax

whether config is TS/YAML/JSON

whether mines get manifests

whether/when a lockfile exists

exact check aggregation behavior

exact update version semantics

exact Prettier preset format

whether leftium-logo becomes library vs CLI

internal add-on API/module boundaries

That prevents an agent from treating speculative sections as requirements.

One v0 question we could decide now, but don't need to

What should the built-in defaults actually be?

For example:

license:
  default = ? MIT?

gitattributes:
  default = leftium
    ├── nodiff
    └── ???

pages:
  no meaningful preset; detect project

I don't think that should block saving the spec. We can put placeholders such as:

Default preset: TBD

and choose them while implementing each add-on.

I'd also add a status legend

Since the spec now mixes committed decisions with future ideas, I'd add something near the top like:

Requirement levels

MUST / SHOULD / MAY
  normative behavior

v0
  required for initial implementation

post-v0
  intended direction, not required initially

provisional
  design idea subject to implementation feedback

That may be the single most useful last edit. The spec has grown organically, and this keeps an agent from spending three days implementing mines, lockfiles, doctor, and logo generation before le add license works.

So: yes, I think we're ready to save it. I’d make the full spec a snapshot of the current architecture, clearly label v0 vs post-v0/provisional, and then let license → gitattributes → pages drive the next revisions rather than doing more speculative design first.

Yes. I think pages-yml + the robots-txt pattern + a reusable workflow is probably the cleanest version of this idea.

I prefer pages-yml over github-pages-yml. It matches robots-txt, describes the artifact you care about (pages.yml), and the README/repo description can remove any ambiguity:

Canonical pages.yml deployment workflow for Leftium GitHub Pages projects.

Your existing robots-txt already has the useful pattern: a canonical source plus a small scripts/update.sh installed into consumer projects. The script fetches the canonical file, validates that it's running in the expected project structure, and supports project-specific overrides. 
GitHub
+1

For Pages, though, reusable workflows give you an opportunity to make it even cleaner.

I would combine them like this
Leftium/pages-yml/
├── README.md
├── CHANGELOG.md
├── .github/
│   └── workflows/
│       └── pages.yml          # actual reusable implementation
├── templates/
│   └── pages.yml              # tiny consumer workflow
└── scripts/
    └── update.sh              # run from consumer project

There are effectively three layers:

                pages-yml repo

        reusable implementation
      .github/workflows/pages.yml
                  │
                  │ @v1.2.0
                  ▼
       consumer .github/workflows/pages.yml
                  ▲
                  │
           scripts/update.sh
                  ▲
                  │
                human
               / agent
1. Reusable workflow = implementation

This is where all the annoying GitHub Pages machinery lives:

YAML
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      artifact-path:
        type: string
        required: true

jobs:
  deploy:
    # checkout
    # install
    # build
    # configure-pages
    # upload-pages-artifact
    # deploy-pages

GitHub explicitly intends reusable workflows for centralizing this sort of deterministic repeated logic. actions/checkout inside the reusable workflow checks out the calling repository, which is exactly what you want. 
GitHub Docs
+1

2. Consumer pages.yml = configuration

Each actual project retains a very small .github/workflows/pages.yml.

Something like:

YAML
# Managed by https://github.com/Leftium/pages-yml
# pages-yml version: v1.2.0

name: Deploy to GitHub Pages

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

jobs:
  deploy:
    uses: Leftium/pages-yml/.github/workflows/pages.yml@v1.2.0
    with:
      artifact-path: build

This is a nice distinction:

central repo owns policy/implementation

How do we deploy Pages correctly?

consumer owns configuration

When do I deploy?
What directory does this project produce?
Which pages-yml version do I use?

GitHub requires reusable workflows to use workflow_call, and external reusable workflows are referenced as owner/repo/.github/workflows/file.yml@ref. 
GitHub Docs

There is one especially important reason I like retaining this little caller file: permissions can't be elevated by the reusable workflow. The caller ultimately controls its token permissions. 
GitHub Docs

So having this visible locally is actually valuable documentation.

3. update.sh = installer / migrator / doctor

This is where I'd borrow most heavily from robots-txt.

Instead of the script being responsible for the deployment, it's responsible for making the consumer repo conform to the standard.

For example:

Bash
bash scripts/update-pages.sh

could:

Detect that it's being run from a Git repo.

Inspect the existing .github/workflows/pages.yml.

Determine its current pages-yml version.

Fetch the current caller template.

Preserve project-specific settings such as:

build output (build, dist, etc.)

branch

package manager

build command, if necessary

Upgrade the caller to the selected/current version.

Tell you what changed.

Optionally run some validation.

You could make it pleasantly explicit:

$ pn pages

pages-yml

project:    Leftium/foo
current:    v1.1.0
latest:     v1.2.0
output:     build

Updating .github/workflows/pages.yml...
✓ workflow updated
✓ configuration preserved
✓ pages-yml v1.2.0

Or:

$ pn pages --check

pages-yml v1.1.0 → v1.2.0 available

That's arguably more useful for Pages than the robots script, because it becomes a migration/diagnostic tool rather than just a file copier.

For pages-yml, I'd make versioning first-class from day one.

For example:

GitHub Docs

And this is very agent-friendly

There's an interesting second purpose here.

An agent encountering:

YAML
# Managed by Leftium/pages-yml
# Do not reimplement this deployment locally.
#
# Docs:
# https://github.com/Leftium/pages-yml

immediately knows:

Ah. This weird-looking 15-line workflow is intentionally thin. Don't "improve" it by expanding it into 70 lines copied from GitHub docs.

And when something is wrong, your repository README becomes the canonical knowledge source for both you and the coding agent:

"I need GitHub Pages deployment."
            ↓
     read pages-yml README
            ↓
      run update.sh
            ↓
   inspect thin pages.yml
            ↓
      reusable workflow

That's probably the biggest advantage over treating this as merely a reusable workflow repo.

The reusable workflow standardizes the machine behavior.

The script standardizes adoption/upgrades.

The README standardizes human/agent understanding.

And the caller's @version gives you tracking essentially for free.

So I'd go with Leftium/pages-yml, and I'd deliberately model its UX after Leftium/robots-txt rather than making it a generic "gh-pages-kit."

Yes. I think Homebrew gives us the missing model for third-party presets, and your gitattributes example makes the add-on/preset distinction much clearer.

Add-on vs preset

I’d define them like this:

add-on = knows how to integrate something into a project

preset = says what configuration that add-on should apply

So there is one generic:

Bash
le add gitattributes

but potentially many presets:

Bash
le add gitattributes --preset nodiff
le add gitattributes --preset eol
le add gitattributes --preset nodiff --preset eol

Multiple presets should absolutely be supported. That makes particular sense for .gitattributes, because the concerns are orthogonal.

For example:

gitattributes presets

nodiff
  package-lock.json     text eol=lf diff=nodiff
  pnpm-lock.yaml        text eol=lf diff=nodiff
  *.generated.json      text eol=lf diff=nodiff

eol
  *                     text=auto eol=lf

binary
  *.png                 binary
  *.jpg                 binary

linguist
  generated stuff       linguist-generated=true

Then your personal preset could simply compose them:

leftium
  ├── nodiff
  └── eol

So:

Bash
le add gitattributes

could default to:

Bash
le add gitattributes --preset leftium

but somebody else can use the exact same add-on with completely different policy.

That same architecture works beautifully for Prettier:

prettier add-on

presets:
  leftium
  standard-ish
  no-semi
  tabs
  ...

And this suggests a precedence rule:

add-on defaults
    ↓
preset 1
    ↓
preset 2
    ↓
...
    ↓
project overrides
    ↓
CLI overrides

Later values win when they genuinely conflict.

How does someone define their own preset?

1. Project-local overrides

The simplest case shouldn't require publishing anything.

Something like:

TypeScript
// leftium.config.ts

export default {
  addons: {
    prettier: {
      preset: 'leftium',
      overrides: {
        semi: false
      }
    },

    gitattributes: {
      presets: ['nodiff', 'eol']
    }
  }
};

This solves:

"I normally like Leftium defaults, except this project."

That is analogous to your current robots-txt base + override approach.

And this is now a good reason for a leftium.config.ts that we previously didn't have. It isn't duplicating detectable state; it's recording desired policy.

Someone should be able to define a reusable configuration within the repo:

  presets: {
    gitattributes: {
      generated: {
        // rules...
      }
    }
  }
};

Then:

Bash

Maybe that's useful eventually, though ordinary overrides will cover most one-project cases.

leftium — Project Setup CLI

Apply and maintain project conventions, integrations, and presets through one command.

Package:

leftium

leftium

le

Project setup tends to become fragmented across:

copied files

framework CLIs

package install commands

shell scripts

reusable GitHub workflows

config files

personal conventions

project-specific exceptions

migration instructions

Examples:

sv add prettier
pnpm create @knip/config
cp LICENSE ...
curl ... > robots.txt
edit .gitattributes
edit prettier config
configure GitHub Pages

leftium provides a single interface for these chores.

The project is inspired by:

sv add

Homebrew

Scoop

package managers generally

the existing Leftium/robots-txt

earlier Leftium preset projects

The central idea is:

one CLI
+
small composable add-ons
+
reusable presets
+
local overrides
+
delegation to upstream tooling
2. Goals

leftium SHOULD:

Provide one command for common project setup:

le add <addon>

Work with:

SvelteKit projects

Svelte projects

generic Node projects

other project types where an add-on applies

Support Leftium add-ons such as:

license
gitattributes
pages
robots
prettier
knip
gg
nimble

Allow sv add add-ons to be invoked through le add when the project is compatible.

Prefer official upstream setup mechanisms over reimplementing them.

Support reusable presets.

Support project-specific overrides.

Support configuration at multiple scopes.

Make add-ons idempotent where practical.

Detect existing configuration before modifying it.

Preserve unrelated project configuration.

Support non-interactive use by agents and automation.

Eventually support inspection, updates, and project-health checks.

3. Non-goals

leftium is NOT intended to:

replace package managers

replace sv

require all le add-ons to be usable through sv

build a separate Svelte add-on ecosystem

duplicate good upstream installers

move standalone packages such as gg or nimble.css into this repository

force every project to use identical configuration

initially solve every upgrade/migration problem

initially provide legal/license-compliance analysis

4. Naming

Package:

leftium

Primary executable:

leftium

Short alias:

le

The long form is canonical because:

the unscoped npm package name is available

npx leftium ... is immediately understandable

it avoids depending on availability of the le npm package name

The short alias exists for daily use:

5. Core concepts

There are three distinct concepts.

5.1 Add-on

An add-on defines:

how to add or maintain a capability or convention.

Examples:

license
gitattributes
pages
prettier
knip
robots

An add-on may:

create files

modify files

install packages

call another CLI

configure shared infrastructure

delegate to sv

5.2 Preset

A preset defines:

reusable configuration for an add-on.

Examples:

license:mit
gitattributes:nodiff
gitattributes:eol
prettier:leftium

Presets SHOULD be composable.

Example:

gitattributes:leftium
  ├── nodiff
  └── eol

An add-on may support multiple active presets.

Example:

le add gitattributes \
  --preset nodiff \
  --preset eol
5.3 Override

An override defines:

the final project- or user-specific delta applied after presets.

Example:

preset:
  gitattributes:nodiff

project override:
  add one project-specific generated file

Overrides are intentionally local and are not expected to be reusable.

6. Native-format presets

Presets SHOULD use the most ergonomic representation for the target configuration.

Do not force text-native formats into JSON or TypeScript unnecessarily.

Examples:

gitattributes → .gitattributes syntax
robots        → robots.txt syntax
prettier      → JSON/JS/TS config
pages         → YAML or structured options
license       → native license text

Example .gitattributes preset:

package-lock.json text eol=lf diff=nodiff
pnpm-lock.yaml   text eol=lf diff=nodiff
bun.lock         text eol=lf diff=nodiff

Example robots preset:

User-agent: SomeBot
Disallow: /

Native input does NOT imply naive string concatenation.

Each add-on may parse and merge its native format intelligently.

7.1 Leaf preset

A native-format file containing actual configuration.

Example:

gitattributes/nodiff.gitattributes
7.2 Composite preset

A small metadata file referencing other presets.

Example:

include:
  - nodiff
  - eol

Possible filename:

gitattributes/leftium.preset.yml

This avoids duplicating configuration.
